segments.title: The Danube as frontier, highway, and logistics system
segments.body: Danube forces included organizations administered specifically for the river, even when they were not formally called flotillas. Their composition followed the geography and the conflicts each state expected to fight. Wide river valleys offered comparatively level routes along which armies could move while boats carried supplies beside them. This made the Danube a route for sustaining campaigns as well as moving trade. Engineering, logistics, minesweeping and mobile artillery therefore occupied much of its river forces' work.

evidence.note: Danube geography, army movement and supply, and the engineering, minesweeping and artillery tasks of river forces.

segments.summary: The Danube's role as an industrial and logistical corridor explains why its flotillas emphasized support, engineering, mine clearance, and mobile artillery.

segments.title: Danube headwaters, trade routes and European frontiers
segments.body: The Breg and Brigach meet around Donaueschingen to form the Danube, which runs through Central Europe to the Black Sea. Its length is given as 2,850 kilometres, or 1,770 miles. The river and the waterways around it carried goods into and out of the continent, linking strategic positions and the routes of campaigns. Its breadth made it a useful imperial frontier as well as a highway for trade. The Romanian-Bulgarian border provides an example of a river boundary, although changing river courses complicate such divisions.

evidence.note: The Breg and Brigach confluence, the Danube's length and Black Sea outlet, trade, imperial frontiers and the corrected Romanian-Bulgarian border example.

segments.summary: The Danube's route from its headwaters to the Black Sea links trade and campaigning with the use of a wide river as an imperial frontier.

segments.title: Can small boats travel beyond the Danube's commercial shipping reach?
segments.body: Navigability depends on the size of the vessel. Narrowboat-sized craft can travel farther upstream than large commercial transports. Alex Clarke recalls a friend taking a canal boat far upriver and tentatively places the journey near the river's beginning. That recollection is the basis for the suggested upstream extent.

evidence.note: Different limits for large vessels and small canal boats, with Alex Clarke's recollection of a friend's journey supporting the tentative upstream extent.

segments.summary: Small canal boats can travel farther upstream than heavy commercial shipping, with the suggested reach near the river's beginning based on a personal recollection.
segments.question: Is the Danube navigable only within the reach used by large commercial vessels?
segments.answerShort: Small canal boats can travel farther upstream. The suggestion that they can reach near the river's beginning rests on a recollection of a friend's journey.

segments.title: Roman Danube fleets and the demands of offensive war
segments.body: Separate Roman commands on the Danube supported campaigning beyond the frontier as well as defence along it. The Classis Pannonica and Classis Moesica had to sustain logistics, raids and reconnaissance across an enormous river system. In this interpretation, their consolidation into the Classis Histrica accompanied the empire's retreat from offensive operations. One fleet was a poor substitute for separate commands along nearly 3,000 kilometres of river. The winding course added to the distance and difficulty of supporting operations across the whole system.

evidence.note: The long Danube corridor and the named Roman fleets, including the Classis Histrica.
The Classis Pannonica and Classis Moesica supporting forces advancing beyond the frontier.
Separate commands for offensive operations and the interpretation of later consolidation as a defensive retreat along a long, winding river.

segments.summary: Consolidating two Roman Danube fleets into one is interpreted as a retreat from offensive campaigning and a poor fit for the river's length.

segments.title: Did France maintain a Danube flotilla?
segments.body: France assembled ships for particular Danube campaigns without maintaining a standing river force or building permanent infrastructure. Those temporary deployments did not amount to a permanent flotilla.

evidence.note: French ships assembled for campaigns rather than maintained as a standing flotilla.

segments.summary: French ships deployed on the Danube for individual campaigns without a permanent flotilla or supporting infrastructure.
segments.question: Did France maintain a force on the Danube?
segments.answerShort: French ships appeared for particular campaigns, but France did not maintain a permanent flotilla or supporting infrastructure there.

segments.title: Why Roman supply followed the Danube despite the road network
segments.body: Roman roads did not remove the need for waterborne transport on the scale required to sustain armies. The Danube connected frontier forts and allowed large quantities of supplies to move between them. Grain, wine and metal cargoes were more efficiently carried by boat than by carts. Access through the Black Sea could also avoid difficult routes across mountains. A defensible river frontier therefore offered a supply route alongside its military barrier.

evidence.note: Roman reliance on maritime and river transport, connected forts, Black Sea access and bulk cargoes including grain, wine, metal and ore.

segments.summary: Water transport linked Roman frontier forts and carried bulky supplies more efficiently than carts, while the Black Sea offered an alternative to mountain routes.

segments.title: Why a 747's cargo volume cannot be compared directly with an oil tanker's
segments.body: Comparing the oil carried by an ultra large crude carrier with a fleet of Boeing 747 freighters requires more than matching their internal volumes. An aircraft's cargo-weight limit can prevent it from filling all its available space with oil. The tanker can use its full cargo capacity in the comparison. No final aircraft total is supplied; the example establishes the loading constraint without giving a numerical conversion.

evidence.note: The challenge to compare Boeing 747 freighters with an ultra large crude carrier, with a numerical answer deliberately withheld.
Aircraft cargo weight and internal space impose different limits, preventing the freighter from filling its available volume.

segments.summary: A comparison between Boeing 747 freighters and an ultra large crude carrier must account for aircraft payload limits as well as cargo space.

segments.title: Why paid Roman oarsmen mattered when troops went ashore
segments.body: Roman oarsmen were paid auxiliaries rather than slaves. A ship depended on them for propulsion, making rebellion during an enemy boarding a direct threat. Limited space also restricted the number of additional soldiers a vessel could carry. Sending troops ashore for reconnaissance could otherwise leave only a few men guarding dozens of strong rowers. Paid crews avoided the internal security problem that an enslaved rowing force would create.

evidence.note: Paid auxiliary oarsmen, the danger of rebellion during boarding, limited troop accommodation and the guarding problem when soldiers went ashore.

segments.summary: Paid auxiliary crews helped Roman river vessels send troops ashore without leaving a small guard to control enslaved rowers.

segments.title: Why riverine warfare is usually about logistics before battles
segments.body: Riverine warfare depended on the continuous movement of supplies, with battles occurring much less frequently. Small Roman boats could reach farther upstream than the largest vessels, extending the routes available to an army. Moving troops and fortifying a frontier both required dependable waterborne supply. Bringing heavy guns to a place such as Vienna posed the same logistical question: how could the equipment reach the army?

evidence.note: Small Roman boats reaching upper waterways and the recurring supply requirements of armies, fortifications and heavy guns.

segments.summary: Small boats and dependable supply routes sustained armies, frontier fortifications and heavy artillery, while river battles were comparatively infrequent.

segments.title: Vienna's Danube position and the limits of Ottoman supply
segments.body: Vienna stood at a Danube trade nexus near the limit of Ottoman logistical reach. Control of the river offered control over goods moving into Central Europe and down from the north. That commercial importance helps explain Ottoman efforts to take Vienna and Polish intervention in its defence. Even a large empire's campaigning depended on whether it could move enough supplies upriver. Roman access to the Black Sea likewise enabled further inland movement along the Danube. Castles beside the river could restrict trade and military supply, giving fixed positions influence over a wider area.

evidence.note: Vienna's trade position, Ottoman and Polish interests, limits on upstream supply, Roman Black Sea access and the influence of riverside castles.

segments.summary: Vienna's importance rested on river trade and the difficulty of sustaining an army far upriver, giving its defence consequences across Central Europe.

segments.title: Why Royal Navy sloops belong in river-gunboat history
segments.body: A history limited to vessels formally called gunboats understates the Royal Navy's river presence. Sloops could perform the same role and enter river systems from overseas stations. The label spans the Age of Sail as well as the 1920s and 1930s, so this was not confined to one technical generation of ship. British stations in South America, Africa, and Asia therefore reveal a much wider operational map than a class-name search alone.

evidence.note: Royal Navy sloops serving as gunboats on overseas stations and rivers during the Age of Sail and the interwar period.

segments.summary: Counting ships by function rather than formal class reveals how often Royal Navy sloops provided gunboat presence on rivers around the world.

segments.title: Austria-Hungary formalizes its Danube flotilla after 1866
segments.body: Austria-Hungary's two capitals were linked by the Danube, yet its river forces remained ad hoc until the aftermath of the Austro-Prussian War. Formal organization as part of the navy followed in 1867. The war is characterised as logistically riverine because its campaigns moved from one waterborne supply route to another. The American Civil War provides a parallel for this dependence on rivers during the 1860s. Heavy reliance on motor vehicles came much later, and waterways still carried large quantities of supplies during the Second World War. A permanent river force therefore served a transport system on which the state already depended.

evidence.note: The Danube linking Vienna and Budapest, naval organization in 1867, river supply routes in the Austro-Prussian War and the continuing importance of water transport.

segments.summary: Despite Vienna and Budapest's dependence on the river, Austria-Hungary did not formalize its naval Danube force until 1867.

segments.title: Why Allied target analysis had to recognize Europe's canals
segments.body: Allied target selection in the Second World War shows how easily planners could underestimate water transport. American officers initially emphasized railways and roads because those systems better matched their assumptions about Germany's economy, while the RAF also took time to recognize the scale of canal traffic. The Royal Navy's economic studies and history departments identified major ships being loaded from lighters and river barges rather than conventional quays. Such ships could use their own cranes to lift supplies from barges alongside them. Ports could therefore consist largely of mooring points in a bay or river estuary, without the extensive loading facilities planners expected. Understanding those connections changed both the target list and the facilities that counted as strategically important.

evidence.note: Comparison of American and RAF assumptions with Royal Navy analysis of canals, barges, self-loading ships, and unconventional port facilities.

segments.summary: British and American planners had to account for the continuing importance of European rivers, canals, barges, and self-loading ships when assessing transport targets.

segments.title: The Danube flotilla and the disputed first shots of the First World War
segments.body: Austria-Hungary's organized Danube force included gunboats, patrol boats and miscellaneous vessels. Its actions on the night of 28-29 July 1914 probably included the first shots of the First World War. The identity of the vessel that fired first remains disputed.

evidence.note: Composition of the flotilla and the probable first shots during the night of 28-29 July 1914.
The unresolved dispute over which vessel fired first.

segments.summary: The flotilla's actions on the night of 28-29 July 1914 are identified as the probable opening shots, with the firing vessel disputed.

segments.title: Körös demonstrates the river monitor's artillery role
segments.body: Körös survived six direct hits from a concealed Serbian battery on 4 August 1914 and later served under the name Morava. The monitor took those hits while exposing the camouflaged battery. As built, the 448-ton vessel had a 54-metre hull, a 9-metre beam and a draught of 1.2 metres. Yarrow boilers supplied triple-expansion engines for a speed of 10 knots. Her armament comprised two 4.7-inch guns, two 2.6-inch guns and two machine guns. Belt and bulkhead protection was 50 mm thick, with 19 mm deck armour and 75 mm around the conning tower and gun turrets. These vessels secured supply traffic and carried heavy artillery into areas where wet ground made its movement ashore difficult. Their gunfire could also support an advance before tanks entered service.

evidence.note: Körös's exposure of a concealed battery, later name Morava, dimensions, machinery, armament, armour and mobile artillery role.

segments.summary: Körös combined shallow draught, armour and 4.7-inch guns to protect river traffic and provide mobile heavy artillery.

segments.title: Czechoslovakia puts its river forces under engineers
segments.body: The First Czechoslovak Republic inherited most of its river craft from Austria-Hungary and divided them between Elbe and Danube sections. Both were considered important, although the Danube could accommodate vessels with greater firepower than the transport and reconnaissance craft of the Elbe. In 1921 Czechoslovakia ended its dedicated Elbe force and intended to use Danube vessels there when practical. It combined the river forces under the Fourth Engineering Regiment. Engineers then had control of complete vessels they could modify, while the inherited craft were already obsolescent by the 1920s.

evidence.note: Inherited craft, Elbe and Danube sections, and consolidation under an engineering regiment.

segments.summary: Czechoslovakia inherited Austro-Hungarian craft, divided them between the Elbe and Danube, and then consolidated them under the Fourth Engineering Regiment.

segments.title: The Czechoslovak Legion's improvised fleets in Russia
segments.body: The Czechoslovak Legion operated steamers and an icebreaker from Vladivostok in 1918. It also used steamers on Lake Baikal during its operations across Russia. These forces preceded the legion's withdrawal and the First Czechoslovak Republic's organization of inherited river craft at home.

evidence.note: The legion's steamers and icebreaker at Vladivostok, steamers on Lake Baikal, operations, and withdrawal.

segments.summary: Before Czechoslovakia organized inherited Elbe and Danube craft, its legion had operated steamers and an icebreaker around Vladivostok and Lake Baikal.

segments.title: President Masaryk, Czechoslovakia's lone new river monitor
segments.body: President Masaryk was the only completed member of a proposed pair intended to replace Czechoslovakia's obsolescent inherited river craft. Named for the country's founding president, she was laid down in August 1929 and commissioned in 1932. Her launch date is given tentatively as 1930 or 1931. She originally used steam turbines and Yarrow boilers, then received diesel engines in 1943 while fuel was scarce and the vessel remained useful. Her original armament comprised four 66 mm guns, four heavy machine guns and ten mines. Engineers repeatedly added weapons, and by 1945 her armament included 88 mm guns, a 37 mm gun and 20 mm guns.

evidence.note: The planned pair, commissioning and tentative launch date, original machinery and armament, diesel conversion and later guns.

segments.summary: Czechoslovakia completed one of two planned monitors, then kept President Masaryk useful through new machinery and repeated changes to her armament.

segments.title: President Masaryk's light armour and mixed ammunition supply
segments.body: President Masaryk had a 10 mm belt, 8 mm turret armour and a 5 mm deck. Even a heavy machine gun might penetrate protection this thin, making claims of bulletproof protection questionable. Despite that vulnerability, she was regarded as Czechoslovakia's best answer to the river forces of Yugoslavia, Romania and Hungary in the 1930s. Her 66 mm guns also introduced an ammunition complication because other Czechoslovak gunboats carried Škoda 75 mm weapons. Using the calibre already fitted to those boats would have simplified supply.

evidence.note: Armour thicknesses and qualified doubts about protection against heavy machine guns.
The regional comparison and the objection to mixing 66 mm and 75 mm ammunition across the flotilla.

segments.summary: Thin armour and 66 mm guns alongside other vessels' 75 mm weapons limited protection and complicated ammunition supply.

segments.title: Soviet control of the Danube through Warsaw Pact flotilla policy
segments.body: Czechoslovakia's river organization broke up with the republic in 1939, followed by attempts to re-establish forces in 1946 and 1950. In 1958 the Warsaw Pact formally assigned Danube defence to the Soviet Navy's flotilla and required national flotillas to disband. Control of armed movement on the river also gave the Soviet Union leverage over economies dependent on Danube trade. Former Warsaw Pact countries later re-established some border forces, organized variously as police or naval flotillas.

evidence.note: The 1958 transfer of Danube defense to the Soviet Navy strengthened Soviet strategic control and leverage over river-dependent economies.

segments.summary: Warsaw Pact members were directed to disband national flotillas as defense of the Danube shifted to the Soviet Navy's Danube Flotilla.

segments.title: Hungary's Danube mission centers on mine clearance
segments.body: In 2020 Hungary's river force belonged to the 1st Explosive Ordnance Disposal and River Flotilla Regiment at Újpest military port in Budapest. Its emphasis on minesweepers reflects the need to keep river traffic moving. Wartime aerial mining illustrates the danger: the RAF and Soviet forces dropped mines into European waterways during the Second World War. Mines that broke loose could drift downstream towards friendly troops advancing upriver, as Soviet forces experienced. Placing mines accurately in smaller rivers was also difficult for a Wellington bomber and easier with a Mosquito.

evidence.note: Hungary's 2020 regiment and Újpest base, wartime aerial mining, downstream drift towards Soviet forces and the Wellington-Mosquito comparison.

segments.summary: Hungary's river regiment centres on mine clearance, a task made essential by the disruption that mines can cause to Danube traffic.

segments.title: Hungary moves its flotilla between police and military control
segments.body: Hungary organized a warship group in 1919 and transferred its ships to the Royal Hungarian River Guard under the Interior Ministry in 1929. In 1939 it became the Royal Hungarian Army River Forces under the Defence Ministry, although it retained naval ranks until July 1944. Its wartime organization paired a Budapest patrol-boat regiment, divided into two groups, with a river-security regiment at Novi Sad containing three battalions. The force supported the invasion of Yugoslavia and helped the Kriegsmarine clear aerial mines from the Danube. Keeping the river open sustained trade, supplies and military logistics. Hungary later proved difficult to persuade to disband its river force during the Warsaw Pact era because it regarded national minesweeping capability as indispensable.

evidence.note: Reorganizations in 1919, 1929 and 1939, naval ranks until July 1944, regimental structure, wartime mine clearance and Hungary's insistence on retaining that capability.

segments.summary: Hungary repeatedly reassigned its river force while preserving the minesweeping and security work that made the flotilla difficult to abolish.

segments.title: Why surplus special-operations boats cannot replace Danube minesweepers
segments.body: Hungary's five domestically built AM-2 minesweepers were mostly in reserve, while its Neštin-class vessels had been acquired from Yugoslavia in 1981. Surplus American special-operations craft offered to river forces lacked the equipment needed for minesweeping. Their availability therefore did not solve the problem of replacing purpose-built mine-clearance vessels. A possible approach is a shared replacement programme among Danube states, with construction locally or at Dutch yards experienced in inshore craft. Existing types used crews of roughly seven, so the replacement would not necessarily need many personnel. The river craft could also lay mines and carry eighty fully equipped soldiers, using the Danube as a route for moving troops.

evidence.note: Hungarian minesweeper holdings and reserve status, the mine-clearance limitation of surplus US craft, a possible joint replacement, small crews and the separate troop-transport role.

segments.summary: Surplus special-operations boats lack minesweeping equipment, leaving Danube states with a specialised replacement requirement for their small river craft.

segments.title: Why a crewed river minesweeper may cost less than full autonomy
segments.body: Crowded rivers place minesweepers among merchant vessels and other traffic with human crews. A replacement needs awareness in every direction and the ability to respond to those movements. An uncrewed vessel could provide that capability, but the estimate is that its necessary systems and facilities would still require a craft of roughly 60 tons. The anticipated expense supports retaining a small crew as a practical design option.

evidence.note: A design judgement about crowded rivers, all-round awareness and the anticipated size and cost of an uncrewed minesweeper.

segments.summary: Traffic awareness and the systems needed for an uncrewed vessel make a small crew an attractive option for future Danube minesweepers.

segments.title: Romania builds an enduring Danube force from 1860
segments.body: Romania traces its continuing river force to Prince Alexandru Ioan Cuza's 1860 merger of the Wallachian and Moldavian components. During the 1877-78 War of Independence, its small flotilla included two armed steamers, a purpose-built gunboat and a spar-torpedo boat. Rândunica sank the Ottoman monitor Seyfi during that war. In 1896 King Carol I divided the navy into sea and Danube divisions, with separate crew depots and naval arsenals to support them. Those permanent institutions supported a river force that had continued since 1860. By the 1920s and 1930s, it had become the world's most powerful riverine force in this account.

evidence.note: The 1860 merger, War of Independence flotilla and Rândunica's attack, Carol I's 1896 reorganization and the claim of interwar pre-eminence.

segments.summary: Romania merged Wallachian and Moldavian river forces in 1860, used Rândunica to sink an Ottoman monitor, and built permanent institutions around its flotilla.

segments.title: Why river bends favoured Romania's spar-torpedo boats
segments.body: Romania returned to Yarrow in Britain for more spar-torpedo boats in 1882 after its earlier boat had proved useful. These small craft displaced 12 tons, developed 150 horsepower and could reach 16.5 knots with eight crew. A river bend offered a chance to appear at short range and charge an opponent. That confined setting gave a spar torpedo one of its more promising opportunities.

evidence.note: Romania's return to Yarrow for more spar-torpedo boats in 1882.
The short-range opportunity at a river bend and the boats' displacement, power, speed and crew.

segments.summary: Small, fast spar-torpedo boats could use river bends to approach at short range, making confined waterways a promising setting for the weapon.

segments.title: Romania combines foreign shipyards with assembly at Galați
segments.body: Romania expanded its flotilla through repeated foreign orders. Thames Iron Works supplied Rahova-class gunboats and later orders of small warships, with Romanian demand helping to sustain the British yard for several years. Schichau also supplied vessels from Germany. A British-built torpedo gunboat carried a 47 mm gun and four torpedoes: two spar weapons and two dropped Whitehead torpedoes. Brătianu-class vessels were built in sections in Austria and sent to Galați in Romania for assembly. Procurement therefore involved both completed vessels from foreign yards and sectional construction for assembly at home.

evidence.note: Orders from Thames Iron Works and Schichau, a gunboat's spar and Whitehead torpedoes, and Austrian-built Brătianu-class sections assembled at Galați.

segments.summary: Repeated foreign orders and the assembly of Austrian-built sections at Galați gave Romania several ways to expand its river flotilla.

segments.title: Romanian river firepower at the Battle of Turtucaia
segments.body: Romanian monitors helped oppose the Central Powers' advance towards the Danube Delta and supported the army around Turtucaia. Bulgarian and German forces captured the fortress and many Romanian prisoners. The victory is judged costly because the Bulgarian army lost considerable strength, mobility and experienced officers. Gunboats feature prominently in paintings of the battle, and river firepower was one of Romania's strongest local assets. Romania diverted forces from Transylvania and halted its advance there to secure the threatened Danube front. That diversion also helped German operations against the Romanian offensive. Control of a key river position thus affected the deployment of forces on another front.

evidence.note: River forces at Turtucaia, the costly Central Powers victory and the diversion of Romanian troops from Transylvania.

segments.summary: Romanian river firepower supported a losing defence at Turtucaia, while the threatened Danube front drew troops away from the advance in Transylvania.

segments.title: Small patrol craft protect scarce major warships from routine duties
segments.body: After the First World War Romania absorbed three monitors from the Austro-Hungarian Navy and bought Italian M-class patrol vessels. It also retained seven 50-ton torpedo boats, transferring three to border patrol with only a machine gun each. Removing small ships leaves their patrol duties to other vessels. If modest patrol craft disappear, expensive primary combatants must absorb secondary and tertiary work instead of concentrating on their intended tasks. Keeping smaller vessels available for routine security duties therefore helps preserve the availability of the major combatants.

evidence.note: Postwar Romanian acquisitions and border-patrol boats, followed by the effect of removing smaller vessels on major combatants' duties.

segments.summary: Retaining modest patrol vessels prevents routine security missions from consuming larger, more expensive combatants.

segments.title: Romania's river force from the interwar period to 2025
segments.body: Romania's flotilla was important during the 1924 Tatarbunary Uprising and helped prevent German troops crossing the Danube from Bulgaria after the 1944 coup. River vessels continued to form part of its armed forces after the war. In the force described in January 2025, three Mihail Kogălniceanu-class monitors operated alongside five Smârdan-class armoured patrol ships. Twelve minesweepers and two fast intervention motorboats complemented the heavier vessels. This mix supported army manoeuvre and a continuing armed presence on the river while helping keep traffic moving.

evidence.note: Operations in 1924 and 1944, followed by the force described in January 2025 and its support for movement on the Danube.

segments.summary: Romania retained monitors, armoured patrol ships and minesweepers for river control and army support, with the January 2025 force also including fast intervention motorboats.

segments.title: Romania's monitors and patrol ships carry different gun batteries
segments.body: The larger Mihail Kogălniceanu-class river monitors carry 100 mm guns forward and aft. Their lighter armament includes 30 mm cannon, 14.5 mm machine guns and surface-to-air missiles. The smaller Smârdan-class armoured patrol ships have a single 100 mm gun. The two layouts distinguish the heavier monitors from the more lightly armed vessels operating alongside them.

evidence.note: Three Mihail Kogălniceanu-class monitors and five Smârdan-class armoured patrol ships.
The larger vessels' forward and aft 100 mm guns, lighter cannon, machine guns and surface-to-air missiles.
A single 100 mm gun on the smaller vessels.

segments.summary: Forward and aft 100 mm guns distinguish the larger monitors from smaller patrol vessels carrying one gun of that calibre.

segments.title: How to identify the bow of a modern Romanian monitor
segments.body: The end with the large gun and recognisable bow form appears to be forward. The apparent direction of movement in a formation photograph supports that reading. The larger and smaller vessels in the formation are also distinguished tentatively, so the identification remains a judgement from the photographs.

evidence.note: Tentative bow identification from the gun, hull form and apparent movement in a formation photograph.

segments.summary: The main gun, hull form and apparent movement in a formation photograph suggest which end of a Romanian river vessel is forward.
segments.question: Which end of the Romanian river vessel in the photograph is the bow?
segments.answerShort: The end carrying the large gun and the recognisable bow form appears to be forward, judging also by the vessels' apparent movement in the photograph.

segments.title: A lowered forecastle and the limits of firing over the crew
segments.body: The gun mounting appears too low to fire over crew standing on deck. A crewman near the cannon provides a visual scale for that judgement. The lowered forecastle allows the gun to depress farther.

evidence.note: Tentative assessment of gun height using a crewman for scale, followed by the explanation of the lowered forecastle and gun depression.

segments.summary: A crewman's height suggests the gun cannot fire over people on deck, while the lowered forecastle allows greater gun depression.
